title: Chapter 161 – A Child of Five
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Yue]

The first thing Yue learns about the Hall is that it has a pulse.

She has been deaf for a long time now. Long enough that the silence no longer feels like a wall but like a country, with its own weather and its own roads. In the valley she kept a map of that country in her head. The stove was a low warm throb under her bare feet. The door was a slap of air. A person walking behind her was a faint change in the floor, a pressure on the heel, and she had learned to turn before they touched her shoulder.

In the Hall of Rest the map is much larger.

It lies in the floor and the walls and the curve of the rail, a vast slow throb that she feels in the long bones of her legs. Once a minute, perhaps, it surges. Once a minute it fades. In the first days she thought it was the sleepers, two hundred thousand chests rising and falling together. Now she knows it is not. It is the Gate, down in the dark shaft, drawing breath through a child.

Since the wake, the surge has changed.

It is weaker. It comes later. And between the surge and the fade there is a stumble, a place where the beat catches on something and has to be coaxed back, like a cart wheel dropping into a rut. She has felt it all night. She sat on the cold floor of the Annex with her back against Tao's cot and her palm pressed flat to the boards, and she counted the stumbles, and she did not write the number down because there was nobody awake to read it.

At dawn she counts forty-one in an hour.

She wipes her palm on her smock. It is wet.

* * *

Nurse is already at the book.

She stands at a lectern at the far end of the corridor with the cracked blue ledger open before her, and a stub of brown ink in her hand, and her back as straight as a ruler. Yue stops a few paces behind and watches the pen move. She cannot hear it scratch. She can see the small, steady, reluctant motions of the nib, and the column of figures lengthening down the page.

Gone. Gone. Gone.

She counts. Thirty-one lines, by the time Nurse lifts the pen.

"They went in the night," says Nurse without turning. Yue reads it off the edge of her cheek, the shape of the lips in the lamplight. "Between the third watch and the fourth. I did not wake you."

Yue steps up beside her and takes the slate from her sash. She writes, Because of Ao.

"Because of the Gate." Nurse's mouth is thin. "Because it is dimmer. Because the draw that kept them was pulled, for a quarter of an hour, to wake a child. It is the same sum as before, only now I can see it. Thirty-one in a night. A week ago, one."

We did that.

"You asked a question of a girl in a well," says Nurse, "and she said yes. If there is a sin in it, it is not yours." She closes the ledger very gently. "But I will not tell you that nothing was lost. You would not believe me."

Yue looks at the closed book. She thinks of the thirty-one beds. Thirty-one strangers whose names she will never know, who lay for six hundred years in the blue light and slipped away between one watch and the next, and not one of them was asked.

She takes the chalk and writes the number on the slate and holds it up, because she needs to see it in her own hand.

31.

Then, below it, smaller: I will remember them.

Nurse reads the line. Something in her face gives.

"Then you will have to be the one to do it," she says. "I am very old, and I have a great deal to carry already."

* * *

Ao is awake, and he is a terrible tyrant.

She finds that out at breakfast, which is a bowl of thin rice gruel on the edge of the stove-bench, with Ao sitting on a stack of folded blankets so that his chin reaches the table. He is wearing the duck-hemmed gown. He has a spoon in his fist like a hammer. He looks at Yue as she comes in, and sets down the spoon, and holds out a hand, palm up, with great ceremony.

She does not understand. She stops.

Ao frowns, and does it again, and then points at the slate in her hand.

Yue passes it over. He takes the chalk in his fist, and with enormous concentration, sticking out the tip of his tongue, draws on the black surface a round shape with two dots and a curved line. He turns it round to show her.

A face. A smiling face.

She laughs. She cannot hear the sound of it, but she feels it jolt in her chest, and Ao beams as if he has been given a prize. He taps the face, and taps his own chest, and then, slowly, taps her.

Friend, he mouths. She can read it. It is the easiest word in the world.

Friend, she signs back, with the clumsy gesture the villagers use. She is not sure that he understands. But he nods, very seriously, and picks up his spoon again, and goes on eating.

Across the table, Bell is watching with her chin on her fist and her eyes soft. She says something. It takes Yue a moment to catch it; the lips move fast.

He has taken to you.

He is three, Yue writes. He has taken to the first person who gave him a slate.

It is all anyone wants, says Bell. To be handed a way to say it.

* * *

Bell keeps her promise after breakfast.

It is a plain lesson. Bell sets a clay cup on the stove-bench and a reed beside it and a small flask of warm broth, and then she takes Yue's wrist and turns it palm up, and lays two of her own fingers on the inside.

"Feel that," she says, slowly, so that Yue can follow. "That is a pulse. Not mine. Yours. Count it for me."

Yue counts. It is quick and light, the beat of a hare. She holds up fingers: seventy-two.

"Good. Now this." Bell takes Ao's tiny wrist, and the little boy submits to it with the long-suffering patience of the very young. "Count."

Yue counts. It is slower, and strong, and steady. She holds up eighty-eight.

"Good. You see the difference? A child's heart runs fast. A grown woman's runs slower. An old man's runs slowest of all, and when it begins to skip, you stop what you are doing and you call for me." Bell lifts her head. "You will not need to call for me, of course. You will not hear me answer. So you will have to learn to know what a skip feels like in the hand."

Yue takes Ao's wrist again and settles into it. She closes her eyes. There is the beat. There is a faint warmth under the skin. After a long moment she opens them and writes.

It feels like a small animal trying to get out.

Bell reads it and laughs. "That," she says, "is the best description of a pulse I have ever heard. Do not tell the other healers. They will steal it."

Yue ducks her head to hide a smile. For the first time in days her hands feel useful.

* * *

On the second night of the Hall, before any of this, she had gone alone to the head of the stair and sat on the topmost step in the dark.

She tells herself she went to watch the lamps. It is not true. She went to be near the cold, and the cold mist, and the long black bridge that she is not permitted to walk. She went to be alone with the thing she has not let herself think about.

Pebble.

It has been forty-one days. She has not once felt the little weight of the pebble against her sternum, the soft inward hum, the sense of a presence at the edge of her mind that said, always, I am here. In the valley it had been a warm companion. On the road it had been a map. In the Hall it was a silence deeper than her own.

She knows why. It is holding the Door. The cost she chose, when she asked it to, and she does not regret it; she would choose it again. But the silence has a shape. It is a small, round, patient absence in the place where a voice used to be.

She touches her breastbone through the smock. There is a shallow dent there, where the pebble once rested.

Are you still there? she thinks, into the dark.

Nothing answers. She does not expect it to.

But the mist rolls by, and the lamps burn low, and far below, in the throat of the shaft, the Gate stumbles and recovers. And Yue, who has made her peace with silence, sits very still on the cold stair and feels, for the length of three slow breaths, that something has felt her ask.

* * *

The old man is not allowed out of bed.

That is a rule, and Bell enforces it with a rolling-pin voice and a look that Yue has seen quell a village headman, and Lin Jian takes it with the helpless grace of the thoroughly defeated. He lies on the eighth cot with his hands folded on his chest. His eyes are open and unfocused. The lines in his face have deepened in the night. When Yue sits down on the stool at his side, he turns his head slowly, and smiles.

"I am a very good patient," he says.

You are the worst I have ever seen, writes Yue.

"Bell says the same." He drifts a moment. His eyes close, and open. "I have been thinking about the sixty days."

So have I.

"The tide. Ao says that it is coming up from the Seam, that the beasts have caught the scent of the Hall. If it is true, then the Wall will be the first thing they reach. The Wall, and the valley behind it." His fingers move on the blanket. "Han will not know. Qinghe will not know. There is no way to tell them, and I cannot walk, and—"

Pebble.

"Is dormant. Holding a door."

Then we send someone else.

His eyes sharpen. "Who?"

She does not answer at once. She has been turning it over since the dawn, since the cold reading of the ledger, and she does not like what she has concluded. She writes it down, and for a moment she doesn't show him.

Me, it says.

He reads it. His face does not change. After a long time he says, gently, "You cannot hear the road."

I can feel it. She presses her heel to the floor. Pebble taught me. The ground tells you where it is going, if you ask it. And I know the way back by the stars you showed me, and by the lamps, and by the ring of light. She meets his eyes. You cannot send Bell. She is needed here. You cannot go. I am the only one who can be spared.

"Not yet."

When?

"When the little one is awake." His voice is firm, for the first time that morning. "When Tao is awake, and walking, and has a hand to hold that is not mine. Then we will talk. I do not want you on the road alone with sixty days at your back and the Hall failing behind."

That is not a decision, she writes. That is a delay.

"It is the best one I have."

She considers pressing the point. Then she sees the faint blue light, shifting behind his eyes, and the effort it costs him to hold his head level, and she lets it go.

* * *

Mei speaks to them at noon.

It is Ethan who asks for it. His voice comes through the grille, faint and carefully gentle, and Bell, who can hear it, tells Yue with a few quick strokes on the slate. He wants all of us at the bridge. She wants to talk. Yue is on her feet before the chalk is dry.

The stair is the same. The cold white mist is the same. But the shaft, when they come out onto the platform, has changed. The milky light has thinned. The ropes of brightness that used to climb its walls like vines now rise slower, and fall back, and in the heart of the glass chamber, the man sits with his hands out and his eyes lowered, and the figure in his palms is smaller.

Yue sees it from the end of the bridge, and she stops.

The girl is no longer the size of a child. She is the size of a doll. Her ribbon of light is threadbare and very bright. Where there was a nightgown there is a smudge, and where there was a stubborn chin there is the memory of one, and only the eyes are whole. Dark, steady, a little tired.

I look terrible, says Mei Cole, cheerfully. Don't pretend I don't.

Bell, at Yue's shoulder, makes a sound she turns into a cough.

I'm all right, the girl says. Twenty-two. Papa says it a lot. It was less than the worst, and more than the best, and I'm still here. She tilts her head. I wanted to say thank you. For asking. And I wanted to say yes again. For the next one.

Ethan's whisper is raw. Mei, no. Not yet. Let us wait. Let us see if the Gate steadies—

It won't. Her gaze goes to Jian, who has been carried to the end of the platform on Bell's arm because he would not be left behind. It won't, will it, old one? You looked at the numbers.

Jian's mouth is gray. "I did."

How long?

"If nothing changes, a year. Perhaps less."

And if I don't help?

"Weeks."

Silence. The thin light in the shaft ripples.

Then I'll help, says Mei. It's simple. I'd rather give some of me to someone who can use it than hold all of me for a few weeks longer. Her dark eyes go to Yue, and Yue feels it, the weight of a look. You. The one who can't hear. I've been watching you. You touch the floor to listen. I wonder if you know that I can feel it.

Yue's heart gives a thump.

I'd like to know the next one, says Mei. The little boy with the top. Would you stay with him? He'll be scared. He's five. He won't know what he's lost.

Yes, Yue writes, and holds it up. Her hand is steady.

Good. The doll-sized shape smiles. Then let's go.

* * *

Ao finds her in the corridor with his rabbit, in the gray hour before the lamps are lit.

She is sitting against the wall with her slate on her knee, and he comes and sits beside her without asking, small and warm, and puts the rabbit in her lap as though it were a coin. She looks at it. She looks at him. He points at the slate, and she wipes it clean and holds out the chalk.

He draws a long wavy line. A river, perhaps. Then, under the line, a great many small dark shapes, crowded together, with teeth.

What is that? she writes.

He looks at her, with that sudden stillness that comes over him when the other voice speaks, and she watches his lips as he answers, slowly, in the careful sing-song of a child repeating a lesson.

The Seam is a river. Under the ground. It carries what the world doesn't want. The beasts live in it. They are very old and very hungry. He draws a small circle at the top of the wavy line. Here is the Hall. The beasts don't come up because the Hall is quiet. But when the Gate is loud, or when it is hurt, they smell it.

Hurt like now?

He nods gravely. Like now.

She thinks of the heave under her palms. She thinks of the sixty days and the Wall at the end of them. She writes, with care, Can you stop them?

Ao looks at his drawing for a long time. His lip trembles. When he speaks again the lesson-voice is gone, and what is left is only a child who is three years old and a very long way from home.

I don't know, he says. I only know that I'm supposed to say. I'm sorry.

She sets the chalk down. She puts her arm round the small shoulders, awkwardly, the way she once held a frightened lamb, and he leans into her at once.

It's not your fault, she tells him, with her mouth, and then, because he is watching her lips so hard, she says it again, very slowly. It is not your fault.

* * *

Tao wakes slowly, and he wakes angry.

Yue is kneeling by the cot with both hands round the little cold one. The hum is in her knees, in her teeth. She watches the white ring turn around the rail, and she feels the Gate stumble, and recover, and stumble. Behind her, Nurse is whispering something, and Bell's arm is round Ao to keep him quiet. On the eighth cot, Lin Jian lies with his eyes closed, one hand curled around the rabbit's paw.

She watches the child's face.

It is a small hard face. Sharp chin, level brows, a line between them that no five-year-old should have. When the glow reaches him, the line deepens. His mouth tightens. His breath comes in short, angry sniffs, like a cat that has been picked up by the scruff.

Then he opens his eyes, and they are furious.

He looks at the ceiling. He looks at the lamp. He looks at Yue, and the hand that holds his, and he snatches his fingers away and sits up with his fists clenched and his whole small body quivering.

"Where's my top?" he shouts.

She cannot hear it. She sees it, the open mouth, the red face, the spray of small spit. She holds out the wooden top, which has been lying by his pillow, and he snatches that too and clutches it to his chest.

"Where's Papa?" he shouts. "Where's Ao? Who are you? What did you do?"

Yue lifts her hands. Slowly, palms outward. She mouths, Friend.

"Don't!" Tao screams. She sees the word on his lips, huge and ragged. "Don't say that! I don't know you! Go away!"

A small hand slaps at her. It stings. She lets it. She does not move. She keeps her palms out and her eyes on his and breathes, long and slow, as she once taught a nervous horse, and after a while the slaps grow weaker. The glare crumples. His lip begins to shake.

Across the room, a small voice says, clearly enough that Yue can read it from three yards away, Tao. It's me.

Tao turns his head.

Ao is standing at the foot of the first cot in his duck-hemmed gown, with the rabbit tucked under one arm. He is not smiling. He looks, Yue thinks, like a very small soldier, delivering a very large message.

It's all right, says Ao. We got woken. It's a good thing. The nice lady is Yue. She can't hear. She's not a bad one.

Tao stares at him. His fists loosen, a little.

"Ao?"

Yes.

"You got big."

No. Ao considers this. I'm exactly the same. The room got old.

A shaky, furious, five-year-old laugh bursts out of Tao, and tears come after it, and he throws the top aside and scrambles across the blankets into his brother's arms. Yue sits back on her heels. She feels the shudder of it through the floor, two small bodies colliding. She feels it in her chest.

She finds she is crying, too.

* * *

Before the dusk, the two small boys have their first quarrel.

It is over the top. Tao will not let it go. He clutches it in both hands and shrieks at Ao, who has only asked to hold it, and Yue, who is sitting on the floor with her back to the stove, watches the whole scene unfold in silent pantomime, the red faces, the stamping bare feet, the tiny hands pushing. It is almost funny. It is also, she realizes, the first time she has seen either of them behave like a child who expects to go on living.

Bell steps in. She does not scold. She kneels between them and holds out her palm and says something low, and Tao's chin trembles, and then, slowly, he puts the top on her hand.

She gives it to Ao. Ao looks at it. He turns it over, once.

It's yours, he says, and hands it back.

Tao stares at his brother. His face crumples. He drops the top in his lap and throws both arms round Ao's neck.

Yue looks away to give them privacy, and finds Nurse watching from the doorway with a hand pressed to her mouth. Their eyes meet. Nurse's lips shape a word, and Yue reads it with no difficulty at all.

Home.

* * *

The cost comes later.

It comes at dusk, when the children are asleep in one bed, with Ao's arm over Tao's chest and the rabbit tucked between them, and the lamps in the Annex have been turned down to a coal. Yue is on the floor with her back to the stove. Bell is checking the pulse of the sleeping Tao with two fingers, and Nurse is in the corridor with the ledger, and the old man is breathing on the eighth cot.

The floor stumbles under her.

It is not the Gate. She knows the Gate's pulse by now. This is something else: a longer, slower thing, a heave that rolls out from the center of the dome and breaks against the outer wall. It comes once. A second later it comes again.

She stands. She presses both palms to the floor.

Bell, she signs, urgently, and then, when the healer does not look, she slaps the boards twice with the flat of her hand.

Bell turns.

Something is wrong, Yue writes, quickly, in a hand that shakes. Not here. Far. Lower than the Hall.

Bell's face changes. She crosses the floor in two strides and drops to her knees beside Yue and lays her own palm on the boards, and for a long moment she is still. Then she looks up, and her eyes are wide.

"I cannot feel it," she says. Yue reads it slowly. "But your face says you can."

It's coming up, writes Yue. Slowly. It's very big.

Bell opens her mouth to answer.

And from the grille in the wall, in a voice gone thin and strange and very young, Ethan Cole says, I think that's the Seam.

The lamps in the Annex flicker. Down in the dark, below the Hall, below the shaft and the bridge and the milk-white light, something enormous and patient turns over once in its sleep.

Yue keeps her palm on the floor, and counts, and does not stop counting until the dawn.

Bell sits down beside her without a word and takes her other hand. Neither of them speaks. In the cot behind them, Tao shifts in his sleep and says something small and cross, and Ao, without waking, pats him twice on the chest.

The floor shakes again, a little closer, a little stronger. Yue counts that, too.
